title: Buddhism: loving-kindness
hookLine: may all beings be happy and at ease (Sutta Nipata 1.8)

lines: A MOTHER AND A SLEEPING BABY.
THE PERSON AHEAD OF YOU IN LINE.
cards: Think about the way a mother looks at her newborn asleep. Nothing is being asked of that baby. It hasn't earned anything or done anything useful.
And the love is total: she'd step in front of a truck for it. Now imagine even a small slice of that toward the person ahead of you in line. Toward the driver who cut you off.
Toward every living creature, seen and unseen. It sounds impossible. The Buddha taught that it can be practiced, a little at a time, like a muscle.

teach.b: Metta is Pali, often translated loving-kindness or goodwill. It's related to the word for a friend, so you could also hear it as friendliness: wishing someone well the way a true friend does.
The most well-known teaching on it is a short text in the Sutta Nipata, one of the oldest parts of the Pali Canon, called the discourse on loving-kindness.

Buddhist tradition tells that it was first given to a group of monks who were frightened while meditating in a forest. It begins with character: be capable, upright, gentle, not proud, content with little.
Then it opens out into wishing. May all beings be happy and at ease.

teach.h: SEEN OR UNSEEN, NEAR OR FAR.
teach.b: And it lists them, so no one is left out: weak or strong, tall or short, large or small, seen or unseen, near or far, those already born and those yet to be born. Then comes the picture from the hook.

teach.h: AS A MOTHER GUARDS HER ONLY CHILD.
teach.b: Just as a mother would protect her only child with her own life, so let a person cultivate a boundless heart toward all beings.

teach.h: YOU, A FRIEND, A STRANGER, A FOE.
teach.b: Many Buddhists across schools practice metta in meditation, often in a traditional order: first toward yourself, then someone you love, then someone neutral, then someone difficult, and finally all beings everywhere.

The phrases are simple and often quiet: may you be well, may you be happy, may you be safe. The idea isn't to fake a feeling. It's to keep pointing the heart in a direction, until the direction becomes a habit.

how: Many Buddhists chant the Karaniya Metta Sutta and practice metta meditation, offering goodwill in turn to themselves, a loved one, a neutral person, a difficult person and all beings.

o: goodwill: wishing every being well, like a true friend
a calm detachment from other people's troubles
a duty to stay polite to everyone you happen to meet

p: the picture of a boundless heart
a later step in the practice

s: metta means faking a warm feeling
it's pointing the heart in a direction until it becomes a habit.
the discourse wishes well even to beings not yet born
seen or unseen, near or far, born or yet to be born.
metta practice often begins with yourself
then a loved one, a neutral person, a difficult person, and all beings.

games.q: you're a monk meditating in a forest, and you're frightened. what does the tradition say the Buddha taught?
games.why: tradition says the loving-kindness discourse was first given to frightened monks in a forest: wish all beings well, seen and unseen.

practice: Wish three people well, the way many Buddhists do: first someone easy to love, then someone neutral, like a neighbor or a cashier, then, if you're willing, someone a little difficult, not the hardest person.
To each, inside, offer the traditional wish: may you be well, may you be happy. Then let it spread wider.

wordCard.voice: Metta. Pali for loving-kindness, friendliness, goodwill: wishing all beings happiness, as a mother guards her only child. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: may all beings be well. It's a wish with no one left out. Day two hundred forty-two, done.
